Chapter 9: Excretory System

Explain the function of the nephron in maintaining blood composition (water, pH and ions)

Identify the role of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and aldosterone in water & sodium ion reabsorption, excretion  and blood pressure regulation.
Waste Excretion & Internal Equilibrium
Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment (internal equilibrium) in the body.
Many metabolic processes generate  a number of harmful waste products that must be eliminated or excreted by the body. E.g.:
Carbon dioxide (through cellular respiration)
urea/uric acid (protein/amino acid metabolism)
Bile pigments (fat metabolism)
etc.
Furthermore, many of these processes can cause an imbalance in blood pH and concentration of salts in and other substances in the blood.
Waste Excretion & Internal Equilibrium
The excretory system has three key functions in maintaining homeostasis:
Eliminates wastes (e.g. urea, uric acid, salts, toxins, etc. )
Regulates blood pH
Regulates fluid and salt concentrations of blood
The Urinary Tract (a.k.a. “Renal System”)
Excretion of toxins by the kidneys occurs via the urinary tract, which consists of the bladder, kidneys, ureters, and urethra.
Anatomy of the Urinary Tract
The aorta carries oxygenated blood to the kidneys through the renal arteries.
Wastes and excess water are filtered from the blood by the kidneys, where they are then conducted through ureters to the bladder.
As the bladder begins to fill, receptors in the brain are activated. Eventually, urine will exit the body through the urethra.
Once blood is filtered by the kidneys, it returns to the heart through the renal veins
Anatomy of the Kidneys
A cross-section of the kidney reveals three major regions/layers:
1)  An outer layer of connective tissue
known as the cortex encircles the kidney
2)  An inner layer known as the medulla lies
beneath the cortex
3)  A hollow chamber known as the renal
pelvis joins the kidney with the ureter
The Nephron
Kidneys are composed of millions of slender tubules called nephrons.
Nephrons span the cortex and medulla of each kidney, and act to remove waste products and other solutes from the blood.
They also allow for the reabsorption of water and solutes back into the bloodstream, thereby maintaining homeostasis.
Any solutes & water that are not reabsorbed are excreted in the form of urine.
Nephron Overview
Movement of Blood through Nephrons
Kidneys are composed of millions of slender tubules called nephrons
Small branches from the renal artery known as the afferent arterioles supply the nephrons with blood
The afferent arterioles branch into a group of capillaries known as the glomerulus. The glomerulus acts to filter out certain components of the blood, including water and salts.
Blood leaves the glomerulus by way of the efferent arterioles. It then moves through the peritubular capillaries and eventually exits the kidney via the renal vein.
Movement of Urine through Nephrons
The glomerulus is surrounded by a funnel-like structure called the Bowman’s capsule.
The fluid or “filtrate” that is filtered out of the blood by the glomerulus (again, mostly water & salts) enters the Bowman’s capsule. The capsule tapers to a thin tubule, called the proximal tubule.
Filtrate is carried from the proximal tubule to the loop of Henle, which descends into the medulla of the kidney.
Urine moves through the distal tubule, the last segment of the nephron, into the collecting ducts. These ducts gather urine from many nephrons, which then merge in the pelvis of the kidney.
Formation of Urine
Filtration
Accomplished by the movement of fluid from
the blood into the Bowman’s capsule.
Reabsorption
Involves the transfer of essential solutes and
water from the nephron back into the blood.
Secretion
Involves the transport of materials from the
blood into the nephron
Urine formation is the result of three steps:
Filtration
As blood moves through each nephron of the kidney, it must pass through the glomerulus into the Bowman’s capsule.
The glomerulus acts like a high-pressure filter, allowing only certain substances to enter the Bowman’s capsule and move on into the proximal tubule.

The high pressure in the glomerulus is achieved, by the afferent arteriole staying wider than the efferent arteriole, which increases resistance to blood leaving and raises pressure inside the glomerular capillaries.
Filtration

Glomerular capillaries work like a sieve. They  have pores that let small molecules (like water, salts, glucose, urea and ions) pass through, but block larger molecules (like protein, RBCs, WBCs, and platelets)
The activity of the glomerulus thus explains why red blood cells are not found in the urine of a healthy person.
Note: The fluid in the glomerulus is still considered blood, while the fluid that has passed into the Bowman’s capsule is now considered the filtrate.
Gets into filtrate
(small stuff)
Water
Ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, etc.)
Glucose
Amino acids
Urea
Small wastes
Does NOT get into filtrate
(large stuff)
Red blood cells
White blood cells
Platelets
Large proteins (e.g., albumin)
Most hormones bound to proteins
Filtration
Question:
How would you predict high blood pressure would affect pressure filtration in the kidneys?

If blood pressure is too high, it creates more force on the glomerular walls, causing more fluid and solutes to be pushed out. Over time, this can damage the glomerulus and lead to protein leaking into the urine.
So: higher blood pressure → higher filtration pressure → increased filtration (at first) but potential kidney damage long-term.
What’s that smell?
Urine gets its distinct smell from the urea that passes through the glomerulus.
Urea is derived from excess protein.
Essentially, when you obtain more protein than your cells require, these proteins are broken down into amino acids in your liver.
This results in the production of ammonia, a nitrogenous compound (NH4) that can become toxic if it builds up.
In the liver, two molecules of ammonia are combined with a molecule of CO2 to form urea, which is eventually released into the bloodstream and excreted through the kidneys into your urine.
2)  Reabsorption
Proximal Convoluted Tubule
Reabsorption of water, salt, glucose, potassium, amino acids, and urea begins in the proximal convoluted tubule.
Substances are largely reabsorbed using active transport (requires ATP), except for water (osmosis) and some salts and bicarbonate ions (diffusion)
2)  Reabsorption
Loop of Henle

Even though most of the water is reabsorbed through the proximal tubule, the filtrate needs to be further concentrated.  The Loop of Henle extends down into the extremely salty medulla, which allows for the additional reabsorption of water through a countercurrent exchange.
The descending limb is impermeable to salts, but is permeable to water. As it reaches down into the salty medulla, water is reabsorbed through passive transport.

The ascending limb of the Loop of Henle is impermeable to water, but is permeable to salt. Here, salt (NaCl) is reabsorbed through diffusion (in the lower portion) and active transport (in the upper portion).
Because the two limbs run side-by-side in opposite directions (countercurrent), the salt pumped out of the ascending limb continually draws water out of the descending limb.
2)  Reabsorption
Distal Convoluted Tubule and Collecting Duct
In the distal convoluted tubule, additional water and salt can be reabsorbed if necessary. This requires the action of hormones (aldosterone and ADH)
2)  Reabsorption
Reabsorption of sodium is aided by a hormone known as aldosterone.
Aldosterone makes the distal tubules more permeable to NaCl. As a result, water is also reabsorbed to maintain the osmotic gradient.
Direct reabsorption of water is aided by a hormone known as antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
ADH increases the permeability of the collecting ducts to H2O.
Stimulus for ADH release
Stimulus for aldosterone release
Question:
How would a deficiency in ADH or aldosterone affect the body’s ability to maintain water and salt balance (homeostasis)?
A deficiency in ADH (antidiuretic hormone) would cause the kidneys to reabsorb less water, leading to large volumes of dilute urine, dehydration, and low blood pressure.
A deficiency in aldosterone would reduce sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion, causing loss of sodium and water, low blood pressure, and imbalance of electrolytes.
Caffeine is a diuretic, which is a substance that increases urine output.

Caffeine inhibits the release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which reduces the kidneys' ability to reabsorb water. This leads to increased urine production, which can cause dehydration if fluids are not replenished. The effect is more pronounced in those who are not regular caffeine drinkers, as tolerance develops over time.
Why does caffeine make us pee??
3)  Secretion
Secretion is the movement of wastes from the blood into the proximal tubule, distal tubule, or collecting duct of a nephron.
Secretion into the distal tubule occurs primarily by active transport
Ammonia, excess H+ ions, and minerals are examples of substances that are secreted.
pH is controlled by the secretion of excess hydrogen ions and restoration of bicarbonate ions in the blood.
Filtration and Reabsorption Summary

Kidney Dysfunction
Proper functioning of the kidneys is essential for the body to maintain equilibrium. Many kidney disorders can be diagnosed by analyzing a urine sample.
Urinalysis
pH
Specific gravity
Protein
Sugar
Red Blood Cells
White Blood Cells

Diabetes Mellitus

Diabetes mellitus is caused by inadequate secretion of insulin from islet cells in the pancreas. This affects the function of the kidneys, as insulin is required for cells to absorb glucose from the bloodstream…
Without insulin, blood glucose levels remain higher than necessary, causing much of this glucose to be excreted in the urine.
Because of the osmotic gradient high blood glucose levels creates, water is unable to be reabsorbed into the bloodstream from the nephron (disrupts passive transport of H2O).
As a result, large amounts of water are lost, explaining why individuals with this form of diabetes are often thirsty.
Insulin injections are an effective treatment for diabetes mellitus
Diabetes Insipidus
Diabetes insipidus results from a defect in a different hormone referred to as antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which regulates water reabsorption in the nephron.
ADH makes collecting ducts more permeable to water and allows for increased reabsorption of water into the bloodstream
Without ADH, the nephron becomes less permeable to water, and less H2O is removed from the filtrate
As a result, individuals with diabetes insipidus also produce large volumes of urine (however, their urine does not contain high concentrations of glucose)
Extreme thirst is also a sign of diabetes insipidus
Nephritis

Nephritis is a general term used to describe an array of diseases characterized by inflammation of the nephrons. This is most often the result of some sort of urinary tract infection, with bacteria entering the body through the urethra.
One type of nephritis affects the blood vessels of the glomerulus.

Toxins produced by invading microbes destroy the blood vessels and alter the permeability of the nephron. This causes proteins and other large molecules to pass into the nephron rather than being filtered out.
As a result, the osmotic gradient is altered, drawing water into the nephron.
Individuals with this form of nephritis thus produce large quantities of urine with a high protein concentration.
Kidney Stones
Kidney stones are caused by the precipitation of mineral solutes from the blood. This typically occurs when your urine contains more calcium or uric acid than the fluid in your urine can dilute.
Kidney stones may develop as a result of an unbalanced diet; too much protein, salt, or sugar in addition to inadequate amounts of water can lead to precipitation of these solutes.
The sharp-sided stones can become lodged in the renal pelvis, or they may move down the ureter into the bladder and be excreted through the urine. Either way, kidney stones are extremely painful.
High-energy shockwaves can be used to break the kidney stones into smaller fragments which can be easily passed.
Kidney Dialysis

For people whose kidneys cannot effectively process bodily wastes, a dialysis machine can help restore the proper solute balance. It does so by removing any additional wastes, salt and water from blood to prevent them from building up in the body...
Kidney dialysis is an artificial way to clean the blood when the kidneys can’t.
Your blood is taken out of your body and passed through a dialysis machine.
Inside, it flows next to a semi-permeable membrane.
On the other side of that membrane is dialysis fluid (dialysate) with the right balance of water, salts, and no wastes.
Diffusion moves wastes (like urea) and extra ions out of the blood into the fluid.
Excess water is removed by osmosis.
The cleaned blood is then returned to the body.
So dialysis basically mimics the kidneys by removing wastes and balancing water and electrolytes.
Kidney Dialysis
Peritoneal Dialysis
The cleaning happens inside the body.
Dialysis fluid is put into the abdomen, and the peritoneal membrane (lining of the abdomen) acts as the filter.
Wastes diffuse from blood vessels in the abdomen into the fluid, which is later drained.
Can be done at home, often daily.
Hemodialysis (Regular Dialysis)
Blood is removed from the body, cleaned by a machine using a semi-permeable membrane, and returned.
Happens in a clinic a few times per week.
Uses an external dialyzer (“artificial kidney”).
Key difference:Hemodialysis uses an external machine, while peritoneal dialysis uses the body’s own abdominal lining as the filter.

Muscles Overview
muscle tissue is highly specialized
muscle tissue converts chemical energy into kinetic energy – the energy of movement
all muscles, regardless of type, can contract
when muscles contract, they shorten and when they relax, they lengthen
muscular tissue makes up 35-40 percent of our body weight
There are three types of muscle cells:
Skeletal muscle
Smooth muscle
Cardiac muscle
Skeletal Muscle Cells
found throughout the body, attached to bones
Skeletal muscle cells are tubular, striated (bands of light and dark), and very long.
Have many nuclei.
Because of their thin, elongated structure, skeletal muscle cells are often referred to as fibres rather than cells.
Contraction is voluntary according to the Sliding Filament Model (more on this soon)
notes: striations have to do with the internal structure of the muscle cell which we will talk about shortly
many nuclei because a muscle fibre is actually several cells fused together
muscle contractions in your hands, taking notes

paragraphs: Skeletal Muscle Functions:
supports the body
makes the bones move
helps to maintain a constant body temperature (shivering)
helps to protect the internal organs and stabilize the joints.
Smooth Muscle
Lines the walls of hollow organs (e.g. blood vessels, digestive tract) where it serves to advance the movement of substances (plays key part in peristalsis)
can also be found in the eye and the skin
Does not have the striated appearance (non-striated) of skeletal muscle.
Smooth Muscle
Cells are long, tapered at each end and arranged in parallel lines forming sheets
Each cell has one nucleus
Contraction is involuntary
controlled and relatively slow, but can sustain prolonged contractions without fatiguing.
CARDIAC MUSCLE
Found in the walls of the heart
Cells are tubular and striated and have one nucleus.
Cells are branched, creating a net-like structure
responsible for the rhythmic contractions of the heart
Cardiac Muscle
Contractions are involuntary, followed by a rest period, thus varying the rate of contraction
Generates its own electrical impulses, which spreads rapidly throughout muscle tissue, allowing it to contract without external stimulation.
MUSCLE CELLS
Both smooth muscle and cardiac muscle depend on mitochondrial activity (aerobic respiration) to provide the energy-rich ATP molecules.
Unlike these two, skeletal muscle may be required to contract rapidly and to remain contracted for long periods of time.
Skeletal muscle relies on both aerobic and anaerobic respiration for ATP production.

Role of skeletal muscle in movement
the work of any muscle is done during its contraction
a body part only moves when a muscle contracts which pulls the body part
muscles can only pull, NOT push!
skeletal muscles that permit movements of the skeleton are present in pairs
they are arranged in pairs that work against each other to make a joint move

e.g. bicep / tricep muscles
Role of skeletal muscle in movement
There are over 600 skeletal muscles in the human body!
Structure of Skeletal Muscle
A muscle consist of muscle fibre bundles, each surrounded by a layer of connective tissue, blood vessels and nerves.
Muscle fibres = Muscle cells
Each muscle fibre is made up of many myofibrils, which are composed of two kinds of myofilaments: actin and myosin.
Actin and myosin are responsible for muscle contraction in the Sliding Filament Model
Structure of Skeletal Muscle
SKELETAL MUSCLE
The cell membrane of a muscle fibre is called the sarcolemma.
The cytoplasm of a muscle fibre is called the sarcoplasm.
The endoplasmic reticulum of a muscle fibre is called the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
stores calcium ions (Ca2+) necessary for muscle contraction
MYOFILAMENTS
Actin: A thin contractile protein that forms the filament myosin pulls on during muscle contraction.
Myosin: A thick contractile protein with heads that attach to actin and generate force by pulling the thin filaments.
Sarcomere
Sarcomere: The basic contractile unit of a muscle fiber, stretching from one Z line to the next.
M line: The central line of the sarcomere where thick (myosin) filaments are anchored.
Z line: The boundary of each sarcomere where thin (actin) filaments attach.

notes: write myosin for thick filament and actin for thin filament

paragraphs: Structure of Skeletal Muscle
Sliding Filament Model Intro
Sliding Filament Model
Muscle contraction involves the movement of the thick myosin filaments past the thin actin filaments.
The “heads” of the myosin filaments attach to the actin and then bend and pull the actin filaments toward the middle, making the sarcomere unit shorter (contracted).
When a myofilament contracts the myosin heads move first in a back and inward motion similar to that of flexing your wrist.
Since the actin myofilament is chemically bonded to the myosin head the actin is pulled along with the myosin heads as they flex.
One after another the myosin heads flex and in effect “walk” step by step along the actin.
Each step requires one molecule of ATP to provide the energy to detach and reposition the myosin after each flex.
Sliding Filament Model
When muscle contraction occurs:
the actin filaments slide over the myosin filaments
the Z lines move closer together
the sarcomere shortens
Sliding Filament Model
The myosin can only attach to the actin when the binding sites are exposed.
When a muscle is relaxed the binding sites are blocked by a regulatory protein called tropomyosin.
When a nerve impulse stimulates a muscle, it causes calcium ions (Ca2+) to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Calcium binds to another regulatory protein called troponin, which causes the tropomyosin to be shifted away from the myosin binding sites.
Control of Muscle Contractions
In Summary
Nerve impulse arrives at the neuromuscular junction
A motor neuron releases acetylcholine (ACh).
ACh binds to receptors on the muscle fiber → muscle action potential is generated.
Action potential travels along the sarcolemma
It spreads down into the muscle fiber through the T-tubules.
Calcium release
The action potential triggers the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release Ca²⁺ into the cytosol.
Calcium binds to troponin
Ca²⁺ attaches to troponin, causing a shape change.
This shifts tropomyosin away from actin’s myosin-binding sites.
These sites are now exposed.
Cross-bridge formation
Energized myosin heads (with ADP + Pi attached) bind to exposed sites on actin.
Power stroke
Myosin releases ADP + Pi.
Myosin head pivots, pulling actin inward → sarcomere shortens.
Cross-bridge detachment
ATP binds to myosin → the myosin head releases from actin.
Myosin reactivation
ATP is hydrolyzed (ATP → ADP + Pi), re-cocking the myosin head so it’s ready for another cycle.
Cycle repeats as long as Ca²⁺ and ATP are present
Actin filaments slide toward the center of the sarcomere.
Muscle shortens/produces tension.
Sliding Filament Model and Muscles Summary
Muscle contraction requires ATP which accessed by muscles in the following ways:
1. Stored ATP (used first)
Muscles keep a very small amount of ATP on hand, and this powers only the first 2-6 seconds of contraction.
2. Creatine Phosphate System (used second)
Creatine phosphate donates a phosphate to ADP to quickly make more ATP, providing an extra 10–15 seconds of energy for short, intense activity (like sprinting).
Energy Sources of Muscles
Muscle contraction requires ATP which accessed by muscles in the following ways:
3. Aerobic Cellular Respiration (used third, as long as oxygen is available)

Uses oxygen to break down glucose, fatty acids, or amino acids to produce lots of ATP (roughly 36 per glucose); this powers long-duration, lower-intensity activities and is the main ATP source at rest.
4. Fermentation/Anaerobic Respiration (used as last resort, when oxygen is no longer available)
When oxygen is low, glucose is turned into lactic acid and only 2 ATP are produced; this supports short bursts of activity but causes fatigue and muscle burn.
Energy Sources of Muscles
Oxygen Debt
During fermentation an oxygen debt incurs
This oxygen debt occurs because oxygen is required after anaerobic exercise to convert the built up lactic acid back into pyruvate in the liver

athletes and other people who train increase their # of mitochondria in muscle tissue, as well as their ability to deliver oxygen– fermentation would not be needed as much (less lactic acid builds up – less oxygen debt)
Muscle Twitch
the action of a muscle contracting and then relaxing (a single contraction) which lasts a mere fraction of a second is called a muscle twitch
occurs upon stimulation by a nerve impulse
all muscles metabolize both aerobically and anaerobically, but many use one type over the other
three main types of muscle fibers:
slow twitch fibres - type I
fast twitch fibres (intermediate form) - type IIa
fast twitch fibres - type IIb (IIx)
FAST VS. SLOW TWITCH MUSCLES
Slow-Twitch Fibres (Type I Fibres):
Tend to be aerobic
Contract slowly but resist fatigue (endurance)
They tire only when their fuel supply is gone.
Many mitochondria
Surrounded by dense capillary beds and draw more blood than fast-twitch fibres.
Mitochondria and rich blood supply give dark red appearance
Abundant supply of glycogen means prolonged production of ATP as long as oxygen is available.
Fast-Twitch Fibres (Type II Fibres):
Depend on anaerobic respiration
Vulnerable to lactic acid build-up and muscle fatigue
Adapted for the rapid generation of power (sprinting, weight lifting)
Rich in glycogen
Fewer mitochondria and blood vessels, and thus a white/pale appearance
FAST VS. SLOW TWITCH MUSCLES
Muscle fibre composition of long distance sprinters vs. runners
The muscular (motor) system works with all systems to maintain overall body function, coordination and homeostasis.
Circulatory system

Muscles power the heart, a cardiac muscle that pumps blood throughout the body. Smooth muscles line the walls of blood vessels and help control blood flow. Skeletal muscles help move blood through veins.
Respiratory system
Skeletal muscles drives breathing by contracting the diaphragm and intercostal muscles for the respiratory system. Smooth muscles in bronchi and bronchioles help regulate airflow.
Digestive system
Skeletal muscles aid in chewing and swallowing
Smooth muscles in help move food through the digestive tract through rhythmic muscle contractions (peristalsis)
Excretory system
Supports the excretory system by contracting smooth muscle in the ureters and bladder to move and release urine.
